title: Why live dubbing lags a sentence behind, and how dubbing from buffered audio fixes it
author: Chris Cornell
summary: Disclosure: I work on EarDub, a browser extension that dubs videos into other languages. This post is about a design problem we hit, not a product pitch, but the product comes up at the end. If you've tried a "real-time" video translator that listens to a video and speaks a translation, you've probably noticed the voice runs about one sentence behind the speaker. The person on screen finishes a thought, there's a pause, then the translation starts, and by then the speaker is already on the next point. On a talk or tutorial, that lag makes the dub feel like a bad simultaneous interpreter. This post explains why that happens and the approach we took to remove most of it for videos that have no captions. Why listen-as-it-plays dubbing trails the picture A tool that captures audio as it comes out of the speakers can only work with what has already been played. To translate a sentence well, you need the whole sentence, because word order changes between languages: a German verb can land at the end, and a Japanese sentence can flip the order of a whole clause. So the pipeline has to: wait for the speaker to finish the sentence, run speech recognition on it, translate it, synthesize speech, play it. Steps 2 to 4 take time, and step 1 alone guarantees the dub starts after the original sentence ends. That's the one-sentence lag. You can shorten it by translating partial sentences, but then the translation gets worse, which is the trade-off live interpreters face. Recorded video is different: the player already has the future For recorded video (not live streams), the browser's media player downloads ahead of the playhead. You can see this yourself in any page with a <video> element: const v = document . querySelector ( ' video ' ); for ( let i = 0 ; i < v . buffered . length ; i ++ ) { console . log ( v . buffered . start ( i ), v . buffered . end ( i )); } console . log ( ' playing at ' , v . currentTime ); The buffered ranges usually extend well past currentTime ( MDN: HTMLMediaElement.buffered ). That audio exists before the viewer hears it. If you recognize speech from the audio the player has already loaded, you're working ahead of the viewer instead of behind them. That changes the pipeline: Recognition runs on audio that's ahead of the playhead. Fragments are joined into complete sentences before translation, so you never have to translate half a thought. The translated sentence is synthesized and queued against the original timing, so it can start when the speaker starts that sentence. The viewer gets a dub that starts with the speaker instead of a sentence later. The details that matter in practice A few things we learned building this: Stay a few sentences ahead, not the whole video. Processing an entire video up front means a long wait before anything plays. Keeping a small window ahead of the playhead lets the first sentence start within seconds, and you pause when the video pauses. Seeking resets the window. When someone jumps to a new point, there's nothing prepared there yet, so the first sentence after a jump takes a few seconds. After that, the window refills ahead of playback. Translated sentences don't always fit. A translation can be longer than the original. Cutting it off sounds broken, so we let the voice speed up gently, capped at 1.45x, and never stop a sentence mid-word. At very high playback rates some sentences can't physically fit, so it's better to skip one than to cut one in half. That's why we recommend staying at 1.5x video speed or below while dubbing. Context beats word-for-word. Translating each sentence with the video's title and surrounding sentences as context keeps names and technical terms consistent across a long tutorial. Know what it can't do. Working ahead requires a recorded video, so live streams are out. Loud music, overlapping speakers and heavy accents still cause recognition errors. One voice reads everyone, because recognized speech doesn't say who is talking. Captions first, audio when there are none When a video already has captions, including auto-generated ones, you don't need speech recognition at all. The caption timing tells you exactly when each sentence starts. Audio recognition is the fallback for videos without captions. Where this ended up This is how EarDub handles videos without captions on YouTube, X, Bilibili and Gumroad (on its paid plans). Captioned videos work on the free plan, including Udemy and Coursera lectures. Audio sent for recognition is processed into text and not stored. If you want to try it, the user-facing details are on the EarDub site, and the extension is on the Chrome Web Store . I'd love to hear from anyone who has worked on similar timing problems, especially sentence segmentation for languages without spaces between words.

title: Lovable App Not Working? What Breaks Between the Demo and Production
author: Tushar Bhendarkar
summary: The Lovable apps in the most trouble were the ones that looked fine. I went through 264 public reports of Lovable apps breaking, from Reddit, Trustpilot, GitHub and Hacker News, and sorted each one by what caused it. The biggest groups were logins and database connections (37), Lovable itself being down (33), and apps that couldn't be found on Google (32). Right behind them were 31 reports about data that was exposed or at risk, which is the one problem a working app can hide completely. I've shipped that kind of bug myself. In one of my own products, any logged-in user could see other customers' private data, because the app checked that you were logged in, but not that the data you asked for was yours. Nothing crashed and nobody complained, which is exactly why nobody had noticed. That's the real gap between a demo and production. A demo only has to work for you, on your laptop, while you watch. Production has to work for every user, on every network, when Lovable has a bad day, when your credits run out, and when someone tries to open data that isn't theirs. Below are the causes in the order I'd check them, each with the fix from Lovable's own documentation. I build on Supabase and Stripe myself, the same backend most Lovable apps run on, so I've added what I check on my own apps. At the end is what I found when I ran 53 live Lovable apps through my free checkers. What 264 broken Lovable apps had in common The reports run from 2025 to October 2026: 195 Reddit threads, 22 Trustpilot reviews, and the rest from Lovable's status page, GitHub issues, Hacker News, YouTube and security write-ups. I put each one in a group based on the cause the thread confirmed or, when nobody found one, the main symptom. Data exposure sits near the top, and it is the one cause you cannot see from inside the app. No single cause dominates, which is why "just ask the AI to fix it" fails so often. The top four groups make up about half of all reports, and the AI can't see most of them from inside the editor: an outage, a login setting in Supabase, how Google reads your site, or what a stranger can see in your database. Step 1: check Lovable, not your app When someone reports a published site is down, Lovable's own hosting docs say to check the status page first, and I agree. Open status.lovable.dev before you change anything. It tracks published sites (under Hosting) separately from the editor, so you can tell whether the problem is your app or Lovable. Its public history only covers the last 90 days, and in that window it lists 36 incidents, including previews and publishing failing on August 10, 2026 and published TanStack apps going down on August 4. The expensive mistake is spending credits during an outage. At least four reports lost credits that way, on prompts and builds that failed because Lovable itself was having problems. And if the app fails for one person but not for others, try their phone on mobile data. Two reports turned out to be an internet provider blocking the app. It works in the preview but not on the live site The preview is your working copy. The live site is a snapshot from the last time you published. Lovable's publish docs are blunt about it: edits aren't live until you open the Publish dialog and click Publish changes, and a small dot on the Publish button means you have unpublished changes. Publishing from that dialog costs no credits, even at a zero balance. If the dialog shows "Build errors need fixing" instead, publishing is blocked until the build passes. Sign-in works in the preview, fails on the live site This is the one I'd check first. Lovable's login docs say sign-in that works in the preview but fails on the published app or a custom domain is usually caused by missing Site URL and redirect URLs. On Lovable Cloud they're updated automatically when you publish. On your own Supabase project they aren't, so you have to add your live address yourself. The preview and the live app share one database This surprises people. In Lovable, the preview and the published app use the same backend and the same data, so test records you create in the preview land in your real database. Separate test and live databases were tried in a beta from February 5, 2026, then withdrawn for new Cloud projects on March 24, 2026. Login and database problems Logins and database connections were the biggest group, with 37 reports: Google sign-in breaking, password resets failing, confirmation emails that never arrived, and projects that couldn't connect to Supabase. These are the usual causes: Confirmation emails stop arriving. Lovable's login emails have an hourly sending limit, which is the first thing to check when many people sign up at once, and the default sender often lands in spam. Google sign-in shows Lovable's name. With Lovable Cloud's built-in Google login, the sign-in screen can say Lovable instead of your app. The fix one thread landed on was setting up your own Google OAuth client and consent screen. Auto-confirm is still on. Turning off email confirmation makes testing easier, but Lovable warns it lets anyone sign up with an address they don't own. Turn it back on before launch. The Supabase project is paused. A paused or still-provisioning Supabase project can't be connected to Lovable, according to its Supabase docs . The failure that does not look broken: your data is open Most Lovable apps keep their data in a Supabase database. Each table has access rules, called row level security (RLS), that decide who can read or change which rows. If a rule is missing or too open, anyone who opens your app can read data that isn't theirs, and everything still looks normal to you. Lovable says this plainly. Its security guide calls misconfigured RLS the most common cause of data exposure in Supabase-backed apps, and its Supabase docs tell you to check the rules yourself before going live. It does scan for it: a quick security scan runs on every publish and looks for tables without RLS and rules that let everyone through. But findings don't block publishing unless a workspace admin turns that on, the deeper code review is something you start by hand, and Lovable itself says its scans can't guarantee security. One thread is worth knowing about: users could see each other's data even though RLS showed as enabled, because database functions, views and storage rules can get around it. A green check on one table isn't proof for the whole app. The check I trust is the one I use on my own apps. When I built Client Approvals , I wrote a test that checks one workspace can never see another workspace's requests. You can do the manual version in a few minutes: create two normal accounts, add something private in each, then try to open one account's records while signed in as the other. Both attempts must fail. It worked yesterday, and an AI edit broke it Twenty-one reports describe the same loop: a small fix breaks two working things, and undoing it costs four or five more messages. Lovable's own debugging advice is to use Try to fix once or twice, describe the bug precisely, switch to Plan mode to find the cause, and revert if the fixes have tangled the code. Plan mode costs one credit a message and doesn't change code. Every change creates a version you can restore from the History panel . But reverting restores code only: it doesn't roll back your database or its migrations, so check your data after a revert. My habit is to stop prompting after the second failed fix and read the actual error instead. For a blank published site, Lovable says to paste the browser console error into the chat, because the agent can't see errors outside the preview. Credits ran out, and the backend went to sleep Credits are the production surprise nobody plans for. Lovable's credits page says that when credits run out, building stops, AI features in your live app fail, and the Cloud database, storage and logins pause shortly after. The pages stay up, but anything that needs the backend stops. Adding credits may not restart it: you have to click Wake up under More, Cloud, Overview. Since June 18, 2026, Lovable splits spending into Build credits, for prompting, and Run credits, for hosting and the backend of the live app. That's when people started reporting idle projects draining credits. In one thread, a background job sending email every five seconds kept a near-idle project busy. I learned this on one of my own products: its AI features had no spending limit, so one bad day could cost any amount. I added a hard cap and a switch to turn the feature off. On Lovable, the equivalent is the usage limits and alerts added on October 7, 2026. Set them before you launch, not after the first surprise. It broke when you moved it off Lovable Twenty-three reports were apps that worked on Lovable and broke on Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare. Most trace back to one change: since May 13, 2026, new Lovable apps are built with TanStack Start, which renders pages on a server. Lovable's self-hosting guide says these apps need a host that runs server code. That's why so many exported apps built fine and then returned 404 on every page. Newer apps (TanStack Start): deploy to a host that runs server code, and check which host the build targets. In one report the build defaulted to Cloudflare, and switching it fixed Vercel. Older apps (React and Vite): add a rewrite that sends every path to index.html, or direct links and refreshes return 404. Settings: set VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY on the new host before you build, and add the new domain to your login redirect URLs. What you take with you: exports include your code and database migrations, but not your data or stored files, and built-in AI calls keep running through Lovable's credits until you replace them with your own accounts. Not on Google? What I found on 53 live Lovable apps Thirty-two reports were about search: apps that never showed up on Google, or shared links with the wrong title and picture. Lovable explains the cause on its own blog : apps built before May 2026 send a nearly empty page and draw everything with JavaScript, and link previews are read from that raw page. Lovable now pre-renders those older pages for Google and other verified crawlers, and since July 28, 2026 you can upgrade an older project to server rendering in place, typically for 10 to 35 credits. It also has a free SEO and AI search review that flags a missing sitemap, robots.txt and metadata. I wanted to see what that looks like on real apps, so I took 53 live Lovable apps from Lovable's own pages, Product Hunt, Hacker News and Reddit launch posts, and ran them through my free sitemap checker , Open Graph checker and security headers checker . I only read what any browser receives. Twenty-one apps give Google no list of their pages, and nine still share Lovable's default image. Twenty-one of the 53 had no sitemap at any of the usual addresses, so Google gets no list of their pages. Nine still shared Lovable's default image, so a link to the app shows Lovable's branding instead of its own. Four pointed their share image at a file that doesn't load, and 13 used images over 300 KB, which WhatsApp often skips. Two sitemaps listed pages on addresses that don't respond, one of them a custom domain that no longer loads while the app's lovable.app address still works. Lovable's domain docs list the usual causes: a leftover AAAA record, records left over from the previous host, or Cloudflare proxying the domain (set those records to DNS only). On security, all 53 were on HTTPS, but 51 sent no Content-Security-Policy and 50 could be loaded inside another site's frame. If you host the app yourself, my security headers checker shows which headers to add. What actually changes between a demo and production Every cause in this post has the same shape. The demo worked because it only had to work once, for you. Production has to keep working for strangers, with an empty credit balance, on a bad day for Lovable, and when someone tries data that isn't theirs. I've been caught by a version of this too. One of my own products ran a daily job that published broken content about nine days a month, and nobody was told. It never threw an error. What fixed it wasn't a smarter job: it was checking the result before publishing, and sending an alert when it failed. So before you launch: publish and open the live address in a private window, sign up as a brand-new user, try to open another user's data, set credit limits and alerts, and check what your link looks like when it's shared. If you also build on Base44, I did the same research in why is my Base44 app not working , and there are more guides in Fix an AI-built app . And if you'd rather hand it over, I take these on as client projects: send me the app link and what's broken. Common questions Why does my Lovable app work in the preview but not when published? The live site is a snapshot from your last publish, so open the Publish dialog and click Publish changes; a dot on the Publish button means you have unpublished edits. If sign-in fails only on the live site, your login redirect URLs are probably missing the live address. And remember the preview and the live app share one database. Why is my Lovable app showing a blank page? In the preview, click Refresh, then Shift+Refresh to restart it; a blank preview usually means an error in the app. On the published site, copy the error from your browser console into the chat, because the agent cannot see errors outside the preview. If the blank page is on Vercel or Netlify, see the next answer. Why does my Lovable app break on Vercel or Netlify? Apps created since May 13, 2026 use TanStack Start, which needs a host that runs server code, so a plain static deploy builds and then returns 404. Older React and Vite apps need a rewrite that sends every path to index.html. Either way, set your Supabase variables before the build and add the new domain to your login redirect URLs. Is my Lovable app's data safe? Only if your database access rules (row level security) are right. Lovable runs a quick scan on every publish, but findings do not block publishing by default and Lovable says its scans cannot guarantee security. Test it yourself: sign in as two normal users and try to open each other's records. Both attempts must fail. What happens when Lovable credits run out? The pages stay up, but AI features in the live app fail and the Cloud database, storage and logins pause shortly after. Adding credits may not restart the backend: click Wake up under More, Cloud, Overview. Set usage limits and alerts before launch so it does not happen by surprise. Why is my Lovable app not showing up on Google? Apps built before May 2026 draw their pages with JavaScript. Lovable now pre-renders them for verified crawlers, and you can upgrade an older project to server rendering in place. Run Lovable's free SEO and AI search review, and make sure you have a sitemap: 21 of the 53 live Lovable apps I checked had none. Why do my Lovable app's links show the wrong picture when shared? Lovable uses the share image you set, or a screenshot of the app, and older projects can still carry Lovable's default image: 9 of 53 apps I checked did. Set your own 1200 x 630 image, publish, then refresh the preview in each platform's debugger, since Slack and LinkedIn keep old previews. This post first appeared on tusharbhendarkar.com . I fix apps built with Lovable, Replit, Bolt and Base44, and I build free checkers for live apps. If something here is broken for you, email me at tusharbhendarkar44@gmail.com .

title: Turn Gmail into a Free Serverless Email API in 5 Minutes!
author: Scott Windon
summary:
Every side project or simple client build ends up needing the exact same thing: a dead-simple way to send transactional emails. Whether it is a contact form on a static site, a failure alert from a cron job, or a notification ping from a small internal tool, you almost always need an API endpoint to fire off an email. The problem is the modern email API landscape for small projects has gotten annoying: Big providers now want credit cards upfront just to touch their free tier. Setup involves domain DNS verifications, DKIM, SPF records, and waiting on sandbox approvals. You end up managing API keys, dependencies, and complex SDKs just to send 5 emails a day. If you already have a Google account, you can build and host your own secure REST email API for free in about 80 lines of Google Apps Script. No credit card, no server maintenance, and no domain DNS config required. Here is what it is, how it works, what Google gives you for free, and how to set it up. What It Is It is a lightweight Google Apps Script deployed as a serverless Web App that exposes an authenticated HTTP POST endpoint. When your backend or serverless function sends a JSON payload to the endpoint, the script validates a bearer token stored in your Google Script Properties and sends the email straight from your Gmail or Google Workspace account using Google's native MailApp service. It supports: Simple JSON over HTTP POST Token-based bearer authentication Plain text and HTML emails Custom sender display names CC, BCC, and Reply-To headers Returning your remaining daily recipient quota directly in the API response What You Get for Free Google Apps Script runs entirely on Google's infrastructure at zero cost. You do not need to supply billing details or provision a cloud instance. Google provides generous daily email sending quotas based on your account type: Account Type Daily Email Recipient Quota Personal Google Account (@gmail.com) 100 recipients / day Google Workspace (formerly G Suite) 1,500 recipients / day For a personal project, portfolio contact form, or dev monitoring script, 100 free transactional emails every single day is more than enough. If you run it on an existing Workspace account, 1,500 per day covers plenty of early-stage SaaS applications or internal company tools. Even better: because the emails are sent directly through Gmail under your authenticated Google account, inbox deliverability is solid right out of the box without configuring custom SMTP servers. How It Works The entire API is contained in a single Code.gs file. Here is the breakdown of the logic: 1. Generating a Secure Token We store a unique token inside PropertiesService.getScriptProperties() . This acts like an environment variable that persists across executions and is never exposed in the source code or client requests: const TOKEN_KEY = ' AUTH_TOKEN ' function generateToken () { const newToken = Utilities . getUuid () + ' - ' + Utilities . getUuid () PropertiesService . getScriptProperties (). setProperty ( TOKEN_KEY , newToken ) Logger . log ( ' Your Auth Token: ' + newToken ) } Running this function once generates a secure, randomized token and saves it in the script storage. 2. Handling Incoming POST Requests The entry point for web apps in Google Apps Script is doPost(e) . The script parses the incoming JSON, validates the token against the stored property, checks required fields, and sends the message: function doPost ( e ) { try { if ( ! e . postData || ! e . postData . contents ) { return jsonResponse ({ success : false , error : ' Missing request body ' }, 400 ) } const data = JSON . parse ( e . postData . contents ) // Auth check const storedToken = PropertiesService . getScriptProperties (). getProperty ( TOKEN_KEY ) if ( ! storedToken || data . token !== storedToken ) { return jsonResponse ({ success : false , error : ' Invalid or missing auth token ' }, 401 ) } // Required fields check if ( ! data . to || ! data . subject || ( ! data . body && ! data . htmlBody )) { return jsonResponse ({ success : false , error : ' Missing required fields: to, subject, and body (or htmlBody) ' }, 400 ) } // Build optional parameters const options = {} if ( data . htmlBody ) options . htmlBody = data . htmlBody if ( data . cc ) options . cc = data . cc if ( data . bcc ) options . bcc = data . bcc if ( data . replyTo ) options . replyTo = data . replyTo if ( data . name ) options . name = data . name // Send the email via Gmail MailApp . sendEmail ( data . to , data . subject , data . body || '' , options ) // Return success and remaining quota return jsonResponse ({ success : true , message : ' Email sent successfully ' , remainingQuota : MailApp . getRemainingDailyQuota () }) } catch ( err ) { return jsonResponse ({ success : false , error : err . message }, 500 ) } } function jsonResponse ( obj ) { return ContentService . createTextOutput ( JSON . stringify ( obj , null , 2 )) . setMimeType ( ContentService . MimeType . JSON ) } Notice MailApp.getRemainingDailyQuota() . Returning this in the response lets your calling app monitor your usage without guessing where you stand against Google limits. 5-Minute Setup Guide Setting this up takes only a few steps: 1. Create the Script Head over to script.google.com and click New Project . Replace whatever is in the editor with the Code.gs script above. Name your project (e.g. Gmail Email API ). 2. Generate Your Secret Token In the Apps Script toolbar, select generateToken from the function dropdown. Click Run . Google will ask you to review permissions. Authorize the script to access your Gmail account. Open the Execution log (View → Execution log) and copy the generated token string. Store this securely in your .env file. 3. Deploy as a Web App Click Deploy → New deployment (top right). Choose Web app as the deployment type. Configure the options: Description: Production v1 Execute as: Me (your email address) Who has access: Anyone Click Deploy and copy your Web app URL . It will look like this: https://script.google.com/macros/s/AKfycbx.../exec That is your live REST API endpoint. Sending an Email Once deployed, you can trigger emails from any language or framework using a standard HTTP POST request. cURL curl -X POST "https://script.google.com/macros/s/YOUR_DEPLOYMENT_ID/exec" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "token": "YOUR_AUTH_TOKEN", "to": "dev@example.com", "name": "App Monitor", "subject": "System Status Update", "body": "Daily backup completed with zero errors.", "htmlBody": "

System Status Update

Daily backup completed with zero errors.

" }' Node.js / Next.js / Astro const API_URL = process . env . GMAIL_API_URL const API_TOKEN = process . env . GMAIL_API_TOKEN async function sendNotification ({ to , subject , body , htmlBody }) { const res = await fetch ( API_URL , { method : ' POST ' , headers : { ' Content-Type ' : ' application/json ' }, body : JSON . stringify ({ token : API_TOKEN , to , subject , body , htmlBody , name : ' My Service ' }) }) const data = await res . json () if ( ! data . success ) { throw new Error ( data . error || ' Failed to send ' ) } console . log ( `Sent! Remaining quota today: ${ data . remainingQuota } ` ) return data } Python import os import requests def send_email ( to , subject , body ): res = requests . post ( os . environ [ " GMAIL_API_URL " ], json = { " token " : os . environ [ " GMAIL_API_TOKEN " ], " to " : to , " subject " : subject , " body " : body , }, timeout = 15 , ) res . raise_for_status () return res . json () Practical Use Cases This setup is ideal when you want reliable transactional delivery without taking on extra SaaS bills or infrastructure overhead: Static Site Contact Forms: If you run a static site on Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, or GitHub Pages, route your form submission to a serverless backend function that hits your Apps Script endpoint. Build and Deployment Alerts: Hook it into GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or custom webhooks to notify your team when a scheduled build or release succeeds or fails. Server Monitoring & Heartbeats: Drop a quick Python script or curl check on a cheap VPS or Raspberry Pi. If a service drops offline or disk usage hits 90%, fire an alert to your personal inbox. Internal Micro-Tools & Staging Environments: Great for dev and staging environments where you need real emails to test workflows without burning paid quotas on your production email provider. Database Backup Reports: Trigger a daily status summary from your Postgres backup scripts. Limitations and Gotchas to Keep in Mind A quick reminder on practical constraints: Security rule: Always keep your AUTH_TOKEN on a server or behind an edge function. Never put the token inside client-side JavaScript or a public repo. Anyone who gets that token can send email through your account. Attachments: This basic script handles text and HTML bodies. If you need PDF invoices or zip attachments, you would need to extend the script to accept base64-encoded file data and pass them as blobs to MailApp . HTTP Status Codes in Apps Script: Google Apps Script web apps return HTTP 200 or 302 redirects for most ContentService text outputs. The script passes error status codes in jsonResponse , but you should always inspect the success: true/false key in the returned JSON body rather than relying strictly on the HTTP status code. Bulk Marketing: Do not use this for newsletters or cold outreach. Google will throttle or flag accounts that violate standard Gmail usage policies. Keep this strictly for transactional notifications and alerts. Wrap Up If you are sick of configuring third-party email providers for tiny projects, Google Apps Script gives you a dependable, completely free alternative that you can roll out in five minutes. Check out the full repository and documentation here: 👉 swindon/gmail-email-api on GitHub Feel free to star it, fork it, or adapt the payload to your own workflow.

title: Teaching an AI agent what’s blocking the sprint: a ClickUp connector for cognee
author: Priyansh Narang
summary: Most teams have the same problem: the answer to "why is this blocked?" exists, but it's spread across a task status, a custom field, three comments and a Doc someone wrote last month. Nobody reads all of that before stand-up. I wanted an agent that could, so I built a ClickUp connector for cognee , the open-source memory layer for AI agents, as part of Mergetober. It turns tasks, comments and Docs into memory an agent can query, and keeps that memory in sync as the workspace changes. This post is about what it took to make that reliable. The ClickUp API had a few surprises, and two of them only showed up when I tested against a real workspace. Ten lines to a sprint memory import asyncio import cognee from cognee_community_connector_clickup import clickup_source async def main (): await cognee . remember ( clickup_source ( space_ids = [ " 90120001 " ]), # token from CLICKUP_API_TOKEN dataset_name = " sprint_memory " , primary_key = " id " , write_disposition = " merge " , max_rows_per_table = 0 , ) answer = await cognee . search ( query_text = " Which tasks are blocked, and what are they waiting on? " , query_type = cognee . SearchType . GRAPH_COMPLETION , datasets = [ " sprint_memory " ], ) print ( answer ) asyncio . run ( main ()) Authentication is a ClickUp personal API token (avatar → Settings → Apps → API Token → Generate). You choose what to ingest with space_ids , folder_ids or list_ids . Run it again tomorrow and only what changed gets fetched. The catch with ClickUp's hierarchy ClickUp nests everything: Workspace → Space → Folder → List → Task, and each level is its own API call. The obvious implementation walks the whole tree before it sees a single task, and does it again on every sync. ClickUp allows 100 requests per minute, so on a large workspace that walk is most of your budget. The way around it is the filtered team-tasks endpoint, GET /team/{team_id}/task . It returns tasks from every list in the workspace, 100 per page, and accepts a date_updated_gt filter. Each task already carries its list and folder names. The only thing it doesn't name is the Space, so the connector fetches Space names once, caches them in the dlt state, and refreshes them only when a task points at a Space it hasn't seen. On my test workspace that meant one Space lookup on the first sync and zero on every sync after. Custom fields don't return what you see Custom fields are where teams keep the important stuff: severity, components, the reviewer. But the API returns them in a form only ClickUp understands. A dropdown comes back as 2 , labels as a list of option IDs, and a people field as a list of user objects. Feed that straight into a knowledge graph and the agent learns that "Severity is 2". The connector resolves each value through the field's type_config , so the document says "Severity: High". It also handles dates, checkboxes, currency, ratings, locations and progress. Here's the connector's real output for an example task: Each task document also carries status, priority, assignees, tags, its Space / Folder / List location, checklists and every comment. The comment endpoint returns only the 25 newest, so the connector pages back through the rest. ClickUp Docs are synced too, through the v3 Docs API, with nested pages rendered as sections. Two things I only found on a real workspace My test suite passed. Then I pointed the connector at a real ClickUp workspace, and two assumptions turned out to be wrong. 1. date_updated_gt isn't strictly "greater than". I passed the newest task's own timestamp, and ClickUp still returned that task (newest − 1 ms returned it, newest returned it, newest + 1 ms didn't). So every "nothing changed" rerun was re-ingesting the latest task and re-fetching its comments. The fix: skip a task whose timestamp equals the cursor if it's already been ingested, while still picking up a genuinely new task created in that same millisecond. 2. Deleting a comment is invisible. I posted a test comment on a real task and watched the task's date_updated . It moved, so new comments are picked up. Then I deleted the comment, and date_updated stayed exactly the same. A cursor-based sync would have kept that deleted comment in the agent's memory forever. Action in ClickUp Changes date_updated ? How the connector handles it Add a comment Yes (verified live) Next incremental sync Delete a comment No (verified live) Daily comment re-check The fix is a comment re-check, once a day by default. The connector re-reads comments on the tasks in scope, compares them with a fingerprint it stored last time, and re-renders only the tasks whose comments changed. I verified it against the live workspace too: the deleted comment was gone from memory after the next check. What a sync costs These numbers are from my test workspace (12 tasks, 1 Doc). The first sync made 17 requests, most of them comments, one per task. A rerun with nothing changed made 4: the workspace lookup, the incremental listing, the deletion check and the Docs listing. The daily comment re-check costs about one request per task, which is why it runs daily rather than on every sync. Forgetting is part of memory ClickUp has no deletion feed, so every run re-lists the IDs in scope. Tasks and Docs that were deleted, archived or moved out of the selection become tombstone rows ( {"id": ..., "_deleted": true} ). dlt hard-deletes them, and cognee's orphan cleanup removes them from the graph and vector store. Two guards stop a bad day from wiping memory. If a listing comes back empty while items are known, the connector assumes an outage and skips the cleanup. And it only saves its progress after a run fully succeeds, so a crash halfway through just means the next run repeats the work. What it doesn't do (yet) Threaded replies to comments aren't fetched; ClickUp serves them through a separate endpoint per comment. Attachments aren't downloaded. Docs are scoped by their direct parent : selecting a Space includes Docs that live directly in it. What I learned Mocked tests told me the code did what I expected. Only the real API told me whether my expectations were right. Both of the bugs above passed every unit test, because the fake API behaved the way I assumed ClickUp did. Now the fake behaves the way ClickUp actually does, so the tests guard against those bugs coming back. Try it The connector is in review as topoteretes/cognee-community#278 , for issue #4701 . Until it's merged, you can install it from my branch: pip install "cognee-community-connector-clickup @ git+https://github.com/priyansh-narang2308/cognee-community@feature/clickup-connector#subdirectory=packages/connector/clickup" If your team lives in ClickUp, I'd like to hear what you'd ask a sprint agent first.

title: GPT-5.6 Sol Helped Chain 3 Chrome Bugs in 6 Days on $40K of API Calls. Google Paid $250K
author: Gabriel Anhaia
summary: Book: Ship It — the pragmatic startup tech stack Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub A crafted web page, opened in Chrome Beta on Windows, pops up Calculator. That is the demo XBOW attached to the full exploit chain it published on October 13: three bugs, from that page to code execution outside Chrome's sandbox. Google paid $250,000 for it, which XBOW calls "the first under its 2026 new rules" . The cost is the number people will repeat. XBOW's research write-up says the team ran OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol through Codex , and that "reconstructing usage from the archived Codex logs puts the six-day campaign at roughly $40,000 in API charges" ( XBOW ). The announcement credits "OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and its predecessors" across the wider project. The write-up's estimate for the same job before LLMs: "a team of four around 6-9 months." XBOW says "All three bugs in our chain are fixed" . Its news release puts the exposure at "an estimated one billion people running Chrome on Windows globally" , and says "the vulnerabilities were never used against Chrome users" . Three bugs, three walls Chrome's sandbox design treats code in a sandboxed process as possibly hostile, so web content runs inside a sandbox, and V8 adds its own sandbox around its heap. A full chain has to get through every wall. Brendan Dolan-Gavitt's write-up lists the three stages: Stage Component Bug What it gave 1 V8's Maglev compiler A mutable HeapNumber reused during deoptimization Read and write inside V8's pointer-compression cage 2 Blink's animated-WebP decoder Time-of-check/time-of-use: cached frame geometry, swapped bytes after an ArrayBuffer transfer One chosen native write outside the cage 3 Crashpad on Windows A short-read retry that trusted a suspended renderer's page protections Code execution in the unsandboxed crash handler GBHackers' summary lists the fixes as XBOW describes them: stop reusing mutable HeapNumbers, keep WebP output buffers inside bitmap bounds, and cap Crashpad retries at the original request length. The write-up cites Chromium issues 547819997, 548509153 and 545820931. XBOW's news release lists CVE-2026-85045 for the WebP bug and CVE-2026-78952 for the Crashpad bug. It gives no CVE for the V8 bug, and none of XBOW's three posts names the Chrome versions that carry the fixes. Three stages, three walls: V8's cage, the renderer sandbox, then the crash handler outside both. Who did the work In XBOW's account, the agents "searched Chrome's source code, tested ideas, built proofs of concept, and wrote the earliest drafts of the exploit." The people "set the strategy, chose where to look," then "checked the agents' work, and redirected the agents." The blog names four researchers: Brendan Dolan-Gavitt, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee and Willem Pinckaers. The setup is the part worth copying. The team did not ask one agent for an exploit end to end. It ran parallel campaigns with narrower goals: broad vulnerability search, V8 memory corruption, a V8 sandbox escape, a renderer sandbox escape, and integration ( write-up ). Each stage had a clean interface and a backup route. The backup routes got used. The first version of the chain used a Gin bug for its V8 sandbox escape, and that bug duplicated an existing report, issue 542670566. The team swapped in the WebP escape after "a very stressful few hours." An earlier chain had already died when its final stage collided with a bug Google had found internally months before. Dolan-Gavitt draws two lessons. "These kind of invariant violations may be where LLMs shine," he writes, and "you will have more success if you give your agents high-quality examples to follow." He also writes, "we did apply a fair bit of our own human expertise and judgment." So I wouldn't read the $40,000 as what the same chain would cost anyone else. Five narrow campaigns run in parallel, with people choosing targets and joining the stages. $40,000 against months of work Six days and about $40,000 in API charges, set against XBOW's own estimate of 6–9 months for a team of four. For scale, CyberInsider notes that the exploit broker Crowdfense advertises up to $1.5 million for desktop Chrome zero-day chains. That figure is an advertised ceiling; nobody is reported to have paid it here. The announcement, which XBOW's CEO Oege de Moor wrote, makes a prediction: "we believe that within a year, each of the three bugs could be found by agents working on their own." That comes from a company that sells AI offensive security, so weigh it that way. It is not the only one this week. On October 14, curl 8.23.0 shipped fixes for 24 CVEs, and AISLE says its AI-driven audit found 18 of them ( my earlier post breaks down the advisory credits). My reading: the gap between a bug existing and someone finding it is shrinking, and so is the price of finding it. Your patch window shrinks with it. What to change this week Relaunch the browser. Chrome downloads updates in the background, and Google's help page says "the update applies the next time you restart Chrome." XBOW's advice: "when the Update button appears, restart it every time." Find the Chromium you ship. Electron "embeds Chromium and Node.js to bring JavaScript to the desktop." Playwright's docs say "Each version of Playwright needs specific versions of browser binaries to operate." A desktop app, a headless-Chrome scraper or a PDF renderer in a container image gets a browser fix when you bump the package and redeploy, not when Google ships. XBOW's posts don't say which embedders or versions were affected, and stage 3 is Windows crash-handler code, so check your embedder's release notes rather than assuming. In an Electron app, the process docs expose both versions: // In your Electron main process console . log ( ' Chromium ' , process . versions . chrome ); console . log ( ' Electron ' , process . versions . electron ); To get pull requests for those packages every day, Dependabot supports an allow list: # .github/dependabot.yml version : 2 updates : - package-ecosystem : " npm" directory : " /" schedule : interval : " daily" allow : - dependency-name : " electron" - dependency-name : " playwright" - dependency-name : " puppeteer" allow works as a whitelist: this entry checks only those three packages, and every other npm dependency in / stops getting update PRs from it. Use it as-is only in a repo with no other npm entry for that directory. If you already have one, don't add allow to it; set its interval to "daily" instead. Point agents at your own code first. XBOW's closing advice: "assume your applications are exploitable and test your own software before someone else does." If six days and about $40,000 in API charges, plus an expert team, can reach Chrome, your service's parsers and file handlers are a smaller job. What this doesn't show People steered every stage, and the six days sat on top of earlier research and failed submissions, as GBHackers points out . The $40,000 is XBOW's own reconstruction from its Codex logs; nobody has audited it. The billion-person figure is XBOW's exposure estimate: people running Chrome on Windows. The demo ran on signed Chrome Beta. None of XBOW's three posts quotes Google; CyberInsider reports that Google approved the payment on August 31, according to its public issue record. I haven't run any of this myself. If a small team with agents can do this to a browser in a week, what's the first thing in your own stack you'd point them at? Tell me in the comments. If this was useful A fix only reaches your users when your own pipeline ships it. If you bundle a browser in an Electron app or a headless-Chrome service, the patch cadence is yours. Ship It covers the stretch between localhost and production for a small team: hosting, deploys, CI/CD, payments, auth and monitoring. I also build Hermes IDE , a free, source-available app that runs Codex, Claude Code and other CLI agents side by side, each in its own terminal and worktree, on macOS, Windows and Linux ( GitHub ).

title: Arbeitsmoral neu denken: Produktivität hängt davon ab, woran wir arbeiten – nicht wie lange
author: Hugh Foreman
summary: Sind längere Arbeitszeiten ein Zeichen für höhere Produktivität? Während künstliche Intelligenz die Arbeitswelt verändert, müssen Unternehmen weniger auf die reine Arbeitsdauer und stärker darauf achten, wie Arbeitszeit genutzt wird, welche Tätigkeiten echten Mehrwert schaffen und wo sich Prozesse optimieren lassen. Ein Amerikaner beschrieb den kulturellen Unterschied zwischen den USA und Deutschland einmal mit einem einfachen Satz: In den USA lebe man, um zu arbeiten, während man in Deutschland arbeite, um gut zu leben. Diese Beobachtung wirft eine zentrale Frage moderner Unternehmensführung auf: Sollte die Leistung von Mitarbeitern anhand ihrer Arbeitsstunden oder anhand der Tätigkeiten und Ergebnisse bewertet werden, die während dieser Zeit entstehen? David Valdes, der von San Francisco nach München zog und bei Google arbeitet, beschrieb diese unterschiedlichen Einstellungen zur Arbeit in der Süddeutschen Zeitung . Während Arbeit in den USA häufig einen zentralen Stellenwert für berufliche Identität und gesellschaftlichen Status einnimmt, legen Beschäftigte in Deutschland tendenziell mehr Wert darauf, Arbeit und Lebensqualität miteinander zu vereinbaren. Auch die Arbeitszeitstatistik scheint diesen Unterschied zu bestätigen. Laut den im ursprünglichen Artikel genannten OECD-Daten lag die durchschnittliche jährliche Arbeitszeit je Erwerbstätigem im Jahr 2025 in Deutschland bei 1.332 Stunden, in den USA bei 1.800 Stunden. Doch längere Arbeitszeiten bedeuten nicht automatisch höhere Produktivität. Ebenso wenig sind kürzere Arbeitszeiten ein Beweis für geringere Leistungsbereitschaft. Eine Stunde ist zunächst nur eine Zeiteinheit. Sie zeigt, wie lange jemand gearbeitet hat – nicht, was dabei entstanden ist. Warum Tätigkeitserfassung wichtiger ist als reine Zeiterfassung Unternehmen dokumentieren seit Jahrzehnten Anwesenheitszeiten, Arbeitsbeginn, Arbeitsende, Pausen, Urlaub und Überstunden. Dennoch fällt es vielen schwer, genau zu verstehen, wie Mitarbeiter ihre Arbeitszeit tatsächlich nutzen. Wie viel Zeit fließt in Kundenprojekte, Administration, Meetings, Recherche, Entwicklung oder Support? Welche Tätigkeiten schaffen Mehrwert, und welche binden Ressourcen, ohne einen entsprechenden Nutzen zu erzeugen? Wo könnten Automatisierungen wiederkehrende Aufgaben reduzieren, und welche Projekte überschreiten regelmäßig ihre geplanten Budgets? Wer diese Fragen nicht beantworten kann, kennt zwar die Arbeitszeit, versteht aber nicht unbedingt die tatsächliche Arbeit. Ein Beispiel: Ein Entwickler automatisiert innerhalb von fünf Stunden einen Prozess, für den bisher jede Woche zehn Stunden benötigt wurden. Das ist kein Zeichen geringerer Arbeitsleistung, sondern ein messbarer Produktivitätsgewinn. Dasselbe gilt für Berater, die durch Erfahrung schneller Lösungen finden, Unternehmen, die administrative Abläufe vereinfachen, oder Teams, die künstliche Intelligenz (KI) einsetzen, um Recherche und Dokumentation zu beschleunigen. Produktivität entsteht, wenn mit der verfügbaren Zeit mehr sinnvoller Wert geschaffen wird – nicht dadurch, dass möglichst viele Stunden verbraucht werden. Wie künstliche Intelligenz die Produktivitätsmessung verändert Künstliche Intelligenz macht diese Unterscheidung immer wichtiger. Aufgaben wie Texterstellung, Dokumentenzusammenfassungen, Datenanalysen, Programmierung und Informationsrecherche lassen sich heute häufig deutlich schneller erledigen. Unternehmen, die Leistung hauptsächlich anhand der Arbeitszeit bewerten, riskieren jedoch, gerade besonders effiziente Mitarbeiter zu benachteiligen. Wenn jemand eine Aufgabe mithilfe von KI in zwei statt vier Stunden erledigt, kann er nach traditionellen Maßstäben weniger beschäftigt erscheinen – obwohl seine Produktivität gestiegen ist. Die eingesparte Zeit könnte stattdessen in Kundenbetreuung, Innovation, Qualitätsverbesserung, Weiterbildung oder zusätzliche Projekte fließen. Damit diese Vorteile tatsächlich entstehen, müssen Unternehmen nachvollziehen können, welche Tätigkeiten Zeit beanspruchen, wo Effizienzgewinne entstehen und wie frei werdende Kapazitäten sinnvoll eingesetzt werden können. Von der Zeiterfassung zur Tätigkeitserfassung Moderne Zeiterfassung sollte nicht nur dokumentieren, wie viele Stunden Mitarbeiter arbeiten. Sie sollte auch zeigen, welche Tätigkeiten diese Stunden ausfüllen, welche notwendig sind, welche Mehrwert schaffen und welche sich vereinfachen oder automatisieren lassen. Hier wird die Tätigkeitserfassung zu einem praktischen Instrument der Unternehmenssteuerung. Mit timespin erfassen Mitarbeiter ihre Tätigkeiten mithilfe eines physischen Dodekaeder-Würfels. Jede Seite kann für ein bestimmtes Projekt, einen Kunden oder eine Aufgabe stehen. Wechseln Mitarbeiter ihre Tätigkeit, drehen sie den Würfel einfach auf die entsprechende Seite. So lässt sich die Arbeitszeit erfassen, ohne wiederholt Softwarefenster öffnen, Projekte suchen oder Zeiten manuell eingeben zu müssen. Die erfassten Daten werden automatisch synchronisiert und stehen anschließend für Auswertungen, Projektabrechnungen und Kostenkontrolle zur Verfügung. Dieser einfache Ansatz erleichtert es, Tätigkeitswechsel unmittelbar zu dokumentieren und ein klareres Bild davon zu gewinnen, wie sich die verfügbare Arbeitszeit verteilt. Tätigkeitserfassung sollte Prozesse verbessern – nicht Mitarbeiter kontrollieren Eine detaillierte Tätigkeitserfassung darf nicht zu einem Instrument werden, mit dem jede einzelne Minute eines Mitarbeiters bewertet wird. Ihr eigentlicher Nutzen liegt darin, wiederkehrende Muster und Möglichkeiten zur organisatorischen Verbesserung sichtbar zu machen. Wenn ein Entwickler viel Zeit für administrative Aufgaben benötigt, können ineffiziente interne Abläufe die Ursache sein – nicht seine persönliche Leistung. Überschreitet ein Projekt regelmäßig die geplanten Entwicklungsstunden, können fehlerhafte Kalkulationen, unvollständige Spezifikationen oder unterschätzter Abstimmungsaufwand dahinterstecken. Wenn Berater einen großen Teil ihrer Zeit für Dokumentation aufwenden, kann die Automatisierung dieses Prozesses sinnvoller sein, als einfach schnelleres Arbeiten zu verlangen. Tätigkeitsdaten sind in erster Linie Prozessdaten. Richtig eingesetzt, helfen sie Mitarbeitern und Führungskräften dabei, Engpässe zu erkennen, Arbeitsabläufe zu verbessern und fundiertere Entscheidungen zu treffen. Warum projektbasierte Unternehmen mehr Transparenz benötigen Eine präzise Tätigkeitserfassung ist besonders für Agenturen, Kanzleien, Softwareunternehmen, Beratungen, Ingenieurbüros und technische Dienstleister relevant. In diesen Unternehmen ist die verfügbare Arbeitskapazität eine wesentliche wirtschaftliche Ressource. Wenn ein Projekt mit 200 Stunden kalkuliert wurde, tatsächlich aber 320 Stunden benötigt, entsteht ein wirtschaftliches Problem – unabhängig davon, wie engagiert das Team gearbeitet hat. Bei Festpreisprojekten kann jede zusätzliche Stunde die Gewinnmarge verringern, statt zusätzliche Umsätze zu generieren. Eine verlässliche Tätigkeitserfassung ermöglicht Soll-Ist-Vergleiche, eine präzisere Nachkalkulation und realistischere zukünftige Projektbudgets. Über Schnittstellen wie REST-APIs und Datenexporte lassen sich die Informationen außerdem in bestehende ERP-Systeme, Buchhaltungsplattformen und branchenspezifische Software übertragen. So entsteht eine fundierte Datengrundlage für Projektmanagement, Kostenkontrolle und operative Planung. Die Zukunft der Arbeit hängt vom Mehrwert ab – nicht von den Stunden Angesichts von KI, Fachkräftemangel, Homeoffice und veränderten Erwartungen an Arbeitszeiten reicht es nicht mehr aus, ausschließlich darüber zu diskutieren, ob Mitarbeiter 35, 40 oder 45 Stunden pro Woche arbeiten sollten. Unternehmen müssen zunächst verstehen, was innerhalb dieser Stunden geschieht. Die produktivsten Organisationen werden nicht zwangsläufig diejenigen sein, die ihre Mitarbeiter zu längeren Arbeitszeiten bewegen. Erfolgreicher werden Unternehmen sein, die nachvollziehen können, wo Ressourcen eingesetzt werden, welche Tätigkeiten Mehrwert schaffen und wo bessere Prozesse oder Technologien unnötigen Aufwand reduzieren können. Arbeitsmoral sollte deshalb nicht daran gemessen werden, wie lange jemand am Schreibtisch sitzt. Entscheidend ist, wie verantwortungsvoll und effektiv die verfügbare Zeit eingesetzt wird. Die Frage für Unternehmen lautet künftig nicht mehr nur: Wie lange haben wir gearbeitet? Sondern: Woran haben wir gearbeitet, was haben wir erreicht – und war der Zeitaufwand es wert? In einer Wirtschaft, die zunehmend von künstlicher Intelligenz und steigendem Produktivitätsdruck geprägt ist, wird die Antwort auf diese Frage wesentlich wertvoller sein als die Feststellung, wer morgens zuerst im Büro erscheint oder abends zuletzt nach Hause geht.

title: Your Browser Can Do WHAT? 5 AI Features That Actually Work
author: Redman WorkflowAlpha
summary: Everyone's talking about AI, but most of it still feels like a chatbot tab you open and forget. The genuinely useful shift is quieter: AI is moving into the browser, running locally, where your data never leaves the machine. Here are five that actually deliver, not just demo well. 1. Local models via WebGPU WebLLM and similar projects run quantized LLMs entirely in your browser using WebGPU. No API key, no server, no per-token bill. The first load downloads the model weights (a few hundred MB), then inference is local. For privacy-sensitive work — drafting internal docs, summarizing confidential logs — this is a real answer to "where does my data go?" 2. Real-time translation that stays on-device Chrome's built-in translation now runs models locally for many language pairs. The quality gap versus cloud APIs has narrowed enough that for everyday content it's the better trade: instant, free, offline, and nothing gets uploaded. 3. Smart tab grouping and memory reduction Chrome's memory saver and tab groups use on-device heuristics to freeze background tabs and cluster related ones. It's "AI" in the unglamorous sense — pattern recognition running locally — but it directly fights the thing every developer actually feels: the browser eating 8GB of RAM. 4. On-device speech recognition The Web Speech API has matured, and Whisper-based WASM builds now transcribe audio in-browser. For meeting notes or voice-driven coding, you get transcription without piping your voice to someone's cloud. 5. Built-in phishing and permission detection Browsers now flag suspicious sites and over-broad permission requests using local classifiers. It's not flashy, but it's the kind of AI that earns trust by being boring and correct. The pattern Notice what these have in common: they run locally , they're fast because there's no network round-trip, and they cost nothing per use. The AI features that stick are the ones that disappear into the tool rather than demanding attention. Which of these have you actually used day-to-day — and which still feel like demos?

title: AI Fatigue? Yea I Know. Here's How I Set Boundaries That Actually Hold
author: Redman WorkflowAlpha
summary: I hit a wall around month three of "AI for everything." Every tool promised 10x. Every morning brought three new products to evaluate. I was spending more time managing AI tools than doing the work they were supposed to accelerate. Sound familiar? AI fatigue is real, and it's not a motivation problem. It's a signal that your tooling has outpaced your workflow. Here's what actually helped. Stop evaluating, start finishing I set a rule: no new AI tool enters my rotation unless it replaces something I already use. Not "complements" — replaces. This killed 90% of my tool churn overnight. The bar isn't "is this good?" It's "does this make my current setup obsolete?" Use AI at the edges, not the core The tools that stuck all share one trait: they handle the tedious edges of my work, not the core. Autocomplete for boilerplate. Summarizing long threads. First-draft outlines I'll rewrite anyway. The moment AI touches the part of the work where I actually think — architecture, trade-offs, the judgment calls — it slows me down because I'm reviewing instead of building. Batch the "check what's new" I used to read AI news daily. Now I do one weekly pass. Nothing important breaks in 24 hours. The tools that matter are still there in a week, and they're better documented by then. Keep a "good enough" default My default stack is boring and it works: one model for drafting, one for code, the editor's built-in completion. I only pull out something special when a task genuinely warrants it. Most tasks don't. The uncomfortable truth A lot of AI fatigue comes from tools that are fun to try and painful to depend on. The best test isn't the demo — it's whether you'd notice if it disappeared tomorrow. If the answer is no, it's not part of your workflow, it's a subscription. What's your boundary? I'm curious what rules other people have found that hold up past the honeymoon phase.
